title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a content-generation tool for fraud, not as a deployed system that failed internally. Scammers used AI to produce a fabricated news article and, according to reporting, deepfake video or audio of real, named public figures, including a finance journalist and a central bank governor, to lend false credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure mode is impersonation at the content layer: AI-generated material made fraudulent endorsements appear authentic enough to deceive consumers into placing money with an entity that held no financial services license.

The deployment gap here is not inside a corporate AI system but in the broader information environment. No platform-level check stopped the fabricated article or associated advertisements from reaching audiences, and the scale reported by the regulator, nearly twenty thousand scams removed in a single year, indicates that detection is reactive rather than preventive. Catching this earlier would have required either identity-verification controls on content that names and depicts real people, or pre-publication screening capable of flagging fabricated quotes attributed to known figures.

What is not established is who operated Boulder Sparhaven, whether any individuals have been charged or convicted in connection with this specific scheme, and whether the deepfakes described involved video, audio, or only text-based fabrication.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fabricated article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview is among a growing wave of investment scams using artificial intelligence. The fake piece promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, by claiming Bullock stormed out over Kohler's questions about it. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that AI-generated deepfakes of celebrities and politicians are becoming increasingly common and convincing, making these schemes harder to detect.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated figures, alongside Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, Pauline Hanson, and others including businessman Dick Smith and billionaire Gina Rinehart. Scammers now create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through its public registers and warns that small initial payments may be used to build trust before larger fraud occurs.
